items.name: Ohm's law and power
items.doc: Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance (U = R × I); the electrical power is P = U × I. Any two of the four values determine the other two.
items.source: Ohm's law and Joule's law (P = U·I); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Voltage divider
items.doc: Two resistors in series divide the input voltage: V_out = V_in × R2 / (R1 + R2). The output is unloaded; for a divider that drives a load use the loaded voltage divider. The current and power are those of the divider chain itself.
items.source: Voltage divider rule; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.

items.name: Loaded voltage divider
items.doc: A voltage divider that drives a load R_L. The load is in parallel with R2, so V_out = V_in × R_P / (R1 + R_P) with R_P = R2 ∥ R_L. The unloaded output V_nl shows how much the load pulls the voltage down.
items.source: Voltage divider with a load (R2 in parallel with R_L); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.
R_P must be smaller than R2; these values do not fit together (a load always pulls the lower resistance down).

items.name: Current divider
items.doc: Two resistors in parallel share the total current in inverse proportion to their resistance: I_1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2) and I_2 = I × R1 / (R1 + R2). The voltage across both is U = I_1 × R1. The two branch currents alone cannot fix the resistors, only their ratio.
items.source: Current divider rule (Kirchhoff's current law with Ohm's law); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

items.name: Series and parallel resistors
items.doc: Resistors in series add up: R_S = R_1 + R_2 + …. Resistors in parallel combine as 1/R_P = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + …. Enter the values as a list, for example 4k7, 10k, 2k2.
items.source: Series and parallel resistor combination; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Decibel ratio
items.doc: The decibel expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale: G = 20 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for voltages and currents (field quantities) and G = 10 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for power. Choose the quantity first: +20 dB is a factor of 10 for voltages but a factor of 100 for power.
items.source: Definition of the decibel (field quantities 20·log10, power quantities 10·log10), cf. IEC 60027-3 (logarithmic quantities and their units)

items.name: dB levels
items.doc: Absolute levels in decibels: dBm is relative to 1 mW, dBV to 1 V and dBu to 0.7746 V, the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω. From a voltage and a load resistance the power follows; the derived values are shown as dBm, dBV and dBu.
items.source: Definitions: dBm = 10·log10(P / 1 mW), dBV = 20·log10(U / 1 V), dBu = 20·log10(U / 0.7746 V) with 0.7746 V = sqrt(0.6) V (1 mW in 600 Ω); decibel per IEC 60027-3

items.name: Wheatstone bridge
items.doc: A Wheatstone bridge is two voltage dividers side by side: R1 over R2 on the left and R3 over R4 on the right. The bridge voltage V_D between the two midpoints is V_D = V_S × (R2 / (R1 + R2) − R4 / (R3 + R4)). It is zero when R1 × R4 = R2 × R3; R_4b shows the R4 that balances the bridge.
items.source: Wheatstone bridge as two voltage dividers with the balance condition R1·R4 = R2·R3; e.g. C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits (resistance measurement with the Wheatstone bridge)

items.name: Star-delta transform
items.doc: Converts between a star (Y) network of three resistors R_A, R_B, R_C and the equivalent delta (Δ) network R_AB, R_BC, R_CA. Delta to star: R_A = R_AB × R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), and cyclically. Star to delta: R_AB = (R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A) / R_C, and cyclically. Enter either the three delta or the three star resistors.
items.source: Wye-delta (star-delta) transformation; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2
formula: rab = (ra * rb + rb * rc + rc * ra) / rc

items.name: RMS, peak and average
items.doc: Converts between the RMS value, the peak value, the peak-to-peak value and the average of the rectified waveform for a sine, square or triangle wave. The crest factor is V_pk / V_rms and the form factor is V_rms / V_avg; for a sine wave they are √2 and π / (2√2) ≈ 1.1107. The average is the mean of the absolute value (the rectified average), not the mean of the signal, which is zero for a symmetric wave.
items.source: Standard waveform relations: sine rms = peak/√2 and rectified average = 2·peak/π; square rms = rectified average = peak; triangle rms = peak/√3 and rectified average = peak/2 (integration of the waveform); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (signals)

items.name: Charge and energy
items.doc: Charge Q in ampere-hours (1 Ah = 3600 C) and energy E in watt-hours (1 Wh = 3600 J) are related by the voltage: E = Q × U. A 2 Ah cell at 3.7 V holds 7.4 Wh. The nominal voltage is only an average; real batteries deliver less energy at high load.
items.source: Definitions of charge and energy: E = Q·U (1 C·V = 1 J), 1 Ah = 3600 C, 1 Wh = 3600 J; The International System of Units (SI Brochure, BIPM)

items.name: Standard-value combiner
items.doc: Finds resistor values from a standard E series (IEC 60063) that reach a target: the nearest single value, and pairs in series or in parallel whose combined value comes closest. Enter the target resistance and choose the series in the settings (E6 to E192); every combination shows its value and its deviation from the target. In series R = R_1 + R_2, in parallel R = R_1 × R_2 / (R_1 + R_2). Example: 5 kΩ from E12 gives 4.7 kΩ + 270 Ω (−0.6 %) or 10 kΩ parallel to 10 kΩ (exactly 5 kΩ).
items.source: IEC 60063 (preferred number series E3 to E192); series and parallel resistor combination: P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: RC low-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC low-pass passes low frequencies and attenuates high ones. Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = 1 / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output phase is φ = −arctan(f / f_c) (the output lags). Above f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 10 nF give f_c ≈ 1.59 kHz; at 1 kHz the output is 84.7 % of the input (−1.45 dB) and lags by 32.1°. The formulas assume an unloaded output (load resistance much larger than R) and an ideal source.
items.source: First-order RC low-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = 1/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = −arctan(f/f_c); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: RC high-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC high-pass blocks low frequencies and passes high ones (a coupling capacitor with the input resistance behind it). Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = (f / f_c) / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output leads the input by φ = arctan(f_c / f). Below f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 100 nF give f_c ≈ 159 Hz; at 100 Hz the output is 53.2 % of the input (−5.48 dB) and leads by 57.9°. The formulas assume an ideal source and an unloaded output.
items.source: First-order RC high-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = (f/f_c)/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = arctan(f_c/f); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: LC resonance
items.doc: An ideal LC circuit resonates at the Thomson frequency f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)); there the reactances are equal, X_L = X_C = √(L / C) = Z_0, the characteristic impedance. Enter any two of L, C and f_0. Example with the defaults: 100 µH and 1 nF resonate at about 503 kHz (medium-wave band) with Z_0 ≈ 316 Ω. Real coils and capacitors have losses; the RLC calculator gives the quality factor and the bandwidth.
items.source: Thomson's resonance formula f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) and Z_0 = √(L/C); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (resonant circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (frequency response, resonance)

items.name: RLC circuit: Q and bandwidth
items.doc: Resonance of a series or a parallel RLC circuit. Both resonate at f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)). The quality factor is Q = √(L / C) / R for a series circuit (R in series with L and C) and Q = R / √(L / C) for a parallel circuit (R in parallel with L and C, for example a load); the −3 dB bandwidth is BW = f_0 / Q. In the formula the exponent s is +1 for the series and −1 for the parallel circuit. Enter three of the six values; the calculator solves the rest when they determine it (f_0, Q and BW alone do not, because BW = f_0 / Q). Example with the defaults (series circuit): R = 10 Ω, L = 100 µH and C = 1 nF give f_0 ≈ 503 kHz, Q ≈ 31.6 and BW ≈ 15.9 kHz (= R / (2π × L)). For the parallel circuit enter the parallel resistance, for example 10 kΩ, which gives the same Q and BW. A Q below 1 means that the bandwidth is larger than f_0.
items.source: Series and parallel RLC resonance: f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)); series Q = √(L/C)/R, parallel Q = R/√(L/C), BW = f_0/Q; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (series and parallel resonance); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: Q is below 1: the bandwidth is larger than the resonant frequency, the circuit is hardly selective. (For a parallel circuit R is the resistance across the tank.)

items.name: Sallen-Key low-pass (unity gain)
items.doc: Second-order active low-pass in the Sallen-Key topology with unity gain (the op-amp is a voltage follower) and two equal resistors R. C_1 is the capacitor from the junction of the two resistors to the output (feedback), C_2 goes from the non-inverting input to ground. f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × √(C_1 × C_2)) and Q = ½ × √(C_1 / C_2). C_1 = 2 × C_2 gives Q = 0.707 (Butterworth, maximally flat); C_1b shows that C_1 for the present C_2. Enter any three independent values. Example with the defaults: R = 10 kΩ, C_1 = 22 nF and C_2 = 10 nF give f_0 ≈ 1.07 kHz and Q ≈ 0.742. The op-amp is assumed ideal; its bandwidth must be much higher than f_0 and the source impedance low.
items.source: Unity-gain Sallen-Key low-pass with equal resistors: f_0 = 1/(2πR√(C_1C_2)), Q = ½√(C_1/C_2), C_1 the feedback capacitor; R. P. Sallen, E. L. Key: A Practical Method of Designing RC Active Filters, IRE Transactions on Circuit Theory, 1955; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Twin-T notch filter
items.doc: Passive twin-T notch (band-stop) filter: two T networks in parallel between input and output, one of two resistors R with a capacitor 2C to ground, the other of two capacitors C with a resistor R/2 to ground. The transfer function has a zero at f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × C), so the output is (ideally) zero there; R/2 and 2C are the shunt parts. Example with the defaults: R = 31.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF give f_0 ≈ 50.4 Hz, a notch for 50 Hz mains hum (shunt parts 15.8 kΩ and 200 nF). The notch is only deep when the parts match closely (use 1 % resistors and matched capacitors). The passive filter has a low Q (a wide notch) and needs a source impedance much lower than R and a load impedance much higher than R.
items.source: Passive twin-T network (arms R-R-2C and C-C-R/2): transmission zero at f_0 = 1/(2πRC), obtained by nodal analysis; filter textbooks, e.g. P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Pi attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive pi attenuator (π pad): one series resistor R_s between two equal shunt resistors R_p. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_p = Z_0 × (K + 1) / (K − 1) and R_s = Z_0 × (K² − 1) / (2K). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 71.2 Ω and R_p ≈ 96.2 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive pi attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_p = Z_0(K+1)/(K−1), R_s = Z_0(K²−1)/(2K); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_p must be larger than Z_0 for a pi attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: T attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive T attenuator (T pad): two equal series resistors R_s with one shunt resistor R_p to ground between them. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_s = Z_0 × (K − 1) / (K + 1) and R_p = 2 × Z_0 × K / (K² − 1). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 26.0 Ω and R_p ≈ 35.1 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive T attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_s = Z_0(K−1)/(K+1), R_p = 2Z_0K/(K²−1); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_s must be smaller than Z_0 for a T attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: Capacitive reactance
items.doc: A capacitor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C). It falls as the frequency or the capacitance rises: a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies. The current through an ideal capacitor leads the voltage by 90°. Example: 100 nF at 1 kHz has X_C ≈ 1.59 kΩ. ESR, ESL and dielectric losses are ignored.
items.source: Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC) with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Inductive reactance
items.doc: An inductor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_L = 2π × f × L. It rises with the frequency or the inductance: an inductor passes DC and blocks high frequencies. The current through an ideal inductor lags the voltage by 90°. Example: 10 mH at 1 kHz has X_L ≈ 62.8 Ω. Winding resistance and self-capacitance are ignored.
items.source: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Series impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in series with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The reactances are X_L = 2π × f × L and X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C); the net reactance is X = X_L − X_C, the magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²) and the phase φ = arctan(X / R) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. At resonance X = 0 and |Z| = R. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF at 1 kHz give X ≈ −96.3 Ω, |Z| ≈ 138.8 Ω and φ ≈ −43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of series RC, RL and RLC circuits (Z = R + jX, X = ωL − 1/(ωC)); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Parallel impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in parallel with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The admittance is Y = 1/R + j × B with the susceptance B = 2π × f × C − 1 / (2π × f × L); the magnitude is |Z| = 1 / √((1/R)² + B²) and the phase φ = arctan(R × (1 / (2π × f × L) − 2π × f × C)) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). ECalc has no unit for a susceptance, so it shows the equivalent parallel reactance X_p = −1 / B instead; at resonance B = 0, the LC branch is an open circuit and X_p is infinite (shown as –). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF in parallel at 1 kHz give |Z| ≈ 72.0 Ω and φ ≈ +43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of parallel RC, RL and RLC circuits (admittance Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)), Z = 1/Y); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
formula: z = 1 / sqrt(1 / r^2 + (uc * 2 * pi * f * c - ul / (2 * pi * f * l))^2)
phi = atan(r * (ul / (2 * pi * f * l) - uc * 2 * pi * f * c))

items.name: RC time constant
items.doc: A capacitor C charges or discharges through a resistor R with the time constant τ = R × C. In general V_C = V_f + (V_i − V_f) × e^(−t/τ) with the initial voltage V_i and the final voltage V_f. Charging towards the supply voltage V_0 means V_i = 0 and V_f = V_0, so V_C = V_0 × (1 − e^(−t/τ)); discharging from the initial voltage V_0 means V_i = V_0 and V_f = 0, so V_C = V_0 × e^(−t/τ). After 1 τ the capacitor has covered 63.2 % of the way, after 5 τ 99.3 %. Example: 10 kΩ and 100 µF have τ = 1 s; charging from a 5 V supply, V_C is 3.16 V after 1 s. The chart shows V_C from 0 to 5 τ.
items.source: First-order RC step response V_C(t) = V_f + (V_i − V_f)·e^(−t/RC); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 7 (first-order circuits)

checks.warn: V_C is at or beyond the final voltage V_f (V_0 when charging, 0 V when discharging). The capacitor only approaches V_f, so no finite time reaches it.
V_C lies on the far side of the initial voltage V_i: the capacitor starts at V_i and moves towards V_f, so this value would need a negative time.

items.name: Series and parallel capacitors
items.doc: Capacitors in parallel add up: C_P = C_1 + C_2 + …. Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel: 1/C_S = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest capacitor. In series the voltage divides in inverse proportion to the capacitance; polarised capacitors in series need balancing resistors. Enter the values as a list, for example 4.7µ, 10µ, 22µ.
items.source: Series and parallel capacitor combination; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Series and parallel inductors
items.doc: Inductors in series add up: L_S = L_1 + L_2 + …. Inductors in parallel combine like resistors in parallel: 1/L_P = 1/L_1 + 1/L_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest inductor. This holds only while the coils do not couple magnetically; mutual inductance is ignored. Enter the values as a list, for example 1m, 2.2m, 4.7m.
items.source: Series and parallel inductor combination (no mutual coupling); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Capacitor energy and charge
items.doc: The energy stored in a capacitor is E = ½ × C × U² and its charge is Q = C × U; also E = ½ × Q × U = Q² / (2 × C). Any two of the four values determine the other two. Example: 1000 µF at 12 V stores 72 mJ and 12 mC. Large or high-voltage capacitors can keep a dangerous charge long after switch-off: discharge them through a suitable resistor before touching them.
items.source: Energy stored in a capacitor E = ½CU² and charge Q = CU; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Air-core coil (Wheeler)
items.doc: Inductance of a single-layer, close-wound air-core coil (solenoid) by Wheeler's formula: L [µH] = N² × r² / (9 × r + 10 × ℓ), with the mean coil radius r and the winding length ℓ both in inches. In the SI units used here this is L = N² × D² / (50800 × (9 × D + 20 × ℓ)) with the mean diameter D (to the centre of the wire) and the length ℓ in metres. It is accurate to about 1 % for ℓ ≥ 0.8 × r (a coil at least 0.4 diameters long) and becomes rough for shorter coils; it assumes an air core and a wire much thinner than the coil. The wire length is the helix at the mean diameter without leads. Example: 25 turns on a 20 mm diameter, 30 mm long winding give about 6.3 µH.
items.source: H. A. Wheeler: Simple Inductance Formulas for Radio Coils, Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 16, no. 10, October 1928 (single-layer coil L = N²r²/(9r + 10ℓ) in inches and microhenries, accurate to about 1 % for ℓ > 0.8r)

checks.warn: The coil is shorter than 0.4 × its diameter: Wheeler's formula is only a rough estimate here (it is accurate to about 1 % from a length of 0.8 × the radius).

items.name: Toroid inductance (A_L)
items.doc: The inductance of a winding on a ferrite or powdered-iron core follows from the inductance factor A_L of the core: L = A_L × N². Data sheets print A_L in nH per turn² (1 nH/N² corresponds to 1 mH per 1000 turns); enter it with the unit prefix, for example 250n for 250 nH. N counts the turns through the centre of the core. A_L holds for small signals below saturation and is stated with a tolerance, so the result is only as exact as the core. N_w is the turn count rounded up to whole turns. Example: A_L = 250 nH and 20 turns give 100 µH.
items.source: Definition of the inductance factor A_L of a magnetic core, L = A_L·N² (A_L in nH/N² as printed in the data sheets of ferrite and powdered-iron core makers)

items.name: Wire resistance
items.doc: DC resistance of a straight conductor: R = ρ(T) × ℓ / A with ρ(T) = ρ20 × (1 + α × (T − 20 °C)). ρ20 and the temperature coefficient α are those of the selected material at 20 °C: annealed copper per IEC 60028 (ρ20 = 0.017241 Ω·mm²/m, α = 0.00393 1/K); aluminium per IEC 60889, hard-drawn aluminium wire (ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m, the 61 % IACS value, α = 0.00403 1/K); silver is a typical handbook value. Values of real wires vary with purity and alloy. The cross-section can be entered in mm², AWG (ASTM B258) or kcmil. For a two-wire run use twice the one-way length. The linear temperature model is reliable only in a moderate range around 20 °C. Example: 10 m of 1.5 mm² copper at 20 °C have 0.115 Ω.
items.source: R = ρ·ℓ/A with ρ(T) = ρ20·(1 + α·(T − 20 °C)); annealed copper ρ20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (rounded to 0.017241) and α20 = 0.00393 1/K per IEC 60028; aluminium ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (the 61 % IACS value) and α = 0.00403 1/K per IEC 60889 (hard-drawn aluminium wire for overhead line conductors); silver 1.59 nΩ·m with α ≈ 0.0038 1/K as typical handbook values (e.g. CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics); AWG per ASTM B258

checks.warn: The temperature is far from 20 °C (below −50 °C or above 150 °C): the linear temperature model loses accuracy there.

formula: r = rho20 * (1 + tcr * dt) * len / a
